body_markdown:
Let’s play a game of word association. I say “restomod,” and you’ll almost certainly say “911.”


The number of companies updating, backdating, or reimagining the 964-era Porsche seems to grow every day.


Britain’s Theon Design got in on the action relatively early and is now marking its tenth anniversary. Founder Adam Hawley and his team have delivered 34 cars to date (including two to the U.S., with another six States-bound cars under construction), with no two the same.


That, he says, is Theon’s point of difference. “I think our biggest USP \[unique selling proposition\] is how bespoke we are and how far we are willing to go,” he explains. “So, because we truly manufacture these cars to the way people want to have them, they’re almost a fingerprint for each customer.”


Theon’s latest build is a perfect example, but instead of fulfilling one owner’s dreams, it had to satisfy three. Commissioned by a father and his two sons, the brief was for a car with two distinct personalities. Dad wanted a relaxed car for road trips, while his lads were after a more focused machine for blasting along Britain’s B-roads.


As with all of Theon’s builds, it begins with a donor car, and it’s often a case of the scrappier, the better. “We won’t take a donor car that’s pristine, because it’s not about ripping up an old car and just starting again,” says Hawley. “It’s about giving it a new life. We would rather take a tired quarter-of-a-million-mile 964 and give it a new life rather than a 2000-mile garage queen. Because why would you do that? It’s a perfectly good car.”


The donor is stripped right back to bare metal, seam-welded to stiffen the shell, and in almost every example, rebuilt with a wider, lighter carbon-fiber body. Metal panels are an option, but they add time, cost, and weight to the build, so very few have gone down that route.


Nik Berg


Although it’s actually wider than a 964 Turbo, Hawley’s approach to the design is to retain its classic look as much as possible. To that end, the car also has a longer hood based on ’70s 911s, and most cars leave Theon’s facility in Britain’s Motorsport Valley with a ducktail rear spoiler, too. The headlamps are modern, but modified so that the bulbs sit further back, just as they would have done in days gone by. There’s serious attention to detail here.


That’s perhaps even more true inside, which, despite its numerous differences from the original, maintains an OEM feel. Hawley has created a new, more symmetrical dash layout using Theon’s own gauges, but the design could easily have come straight from Stuttgart. Touchpoints from door handles to window switches and to vent controls have been remade in aluminum, while most every surface is swathed in rich baseball glove-like leather to complement the Irish Green paintwork. Green over tan, you really can’t beat it.


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


Theon Design


Theon Design


On[Theon’s configurator](https://theondesign.com/configurator/) , you can give it a good go, though; there are over four quadrillion combinations of colors, materials, and options to choose from. U.S. buyers can also speak to automotive concierge[Humble House](https://humblehouseauto.com/) about Theon builds.


There’s also a choice of power, with 3.6, 3.8 and 4.0-liter naturally-aspirated flat-sixes available. Theon has built a supercharged motor for one customer, but so far has avoided turbocharging. Even the firm’s new limited-to-24, 540-hp, $1.3 M halo car, the R, will be unboosted. It will weigh less than a metric ton (2200 lbs), however, so it’s unlikely that anyone will complain.


Father and sons settled on a four-liter with 415 horsepower from its dry-sumped motor. Carbon-trumpeted Jenvey independent throttle bodies feed the engine, which uses a MoTeC engine management system with drive-by-wire. Talking of wires, Theon’s own loom cuts some 60 lbs out of the car on its own, not least by deleting the factory-installed connections for towing and electric folding roof. Further pounds are lost with a new electric heating and cooling system and electric power steering. Both of these systems are also relocated to the front of the car, which helps create a more balanced 46/54 weight distribution. All up, it weighs 2535 lbs wet.


Theon Design


The family opted for a five-speed Hewland G50 transmission, instead of the closer-ratio six-speed, trading off some acceleration for less shifting and a quieter cruise. It’s perhaps not quite as precise as it could be, but more accuracy might well result in less charm.


The MoTeC management allows for four different maps, in escalating brutality. A city mode effectively only gives 25 percent throttle, and after a few minutes of not unreasonable progress along the country lanes near the workshop, Hawley realizes that that’s the mode the car is actually in. He reaches over, adjusts a dial below the steering wheel, and it’s like pulling a trigger. The Theon explodes forwards, the exhaust valves open and the roadside hedges become a blur. It is blisteringly fast, with Hawley’s estimate of a three-second sprint to 60 mph being confirmed by my own butt dyno. There are two distinct surges along the way, one at 4000 rpm and another at 5500, the idea being that dad can get his kicks lower down while the boys rush to the redline.


It’s a miserably rainy day, yet when I do pop the clutch for a pretty hard launch, the car just digs in and goes. There’s no traction control, but seemingly no need, with only the faintest squirm of those fat rear tires, even at a near-redline upshift.


Theon Design


There’s some devious suspension geometry going here for sure. The TracTive semi-active dampers and KW springs do a remarkable job of maintaining a reasonable ride over some pretty poor surfaces, yet also ensuring the car feels planted at all times. The Wilwood brakes (carbon ceramics are available) are potent and don’t trouble the factory ABS even in this grim weather. The steering, complete with a dishy three-spoke wheel, is as direct as you’d ever want and communicative without being nervy.


It’s only a taster drive, but what’s clear is that the fundamentals of a classic 911 remain. Performance, handling, and quality are all gigantic steps up, but that’s not to say it drives like a modern car.


It takes time (around 18 months) and money (starting from $580,000 plus a donor vehicle) to make this magic happen. Theon’s customers are involved every step of the way, and, to date, nobody has sold one on.


“Our first American customer, he was saying it will be a family heirloom that he’s going to hand down. It’s what a lot of them say. It’s like the whole Patek Philippe watch thing. You’re never the owner. You’re just the custodian.”


One fortunate family will soon be fighting over the keys.


Theon Design
